analysis.one_liner: Extends caps on mortgage interest and foreclosure protections for servicemembers after they leave active duty.
analysis.headline: The bill, aimed at protecting servicemembers from foreclosure as the 2008 housing crisis deepened, was never voted on; it sat in the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee until the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend an existing law that protects active-duty troops financially. It would extend the 6% cap on mortgage interest to one year after a servicemember leaves active duty, instead of only during service. It would also extend foreclosure protections from 90 days to one year after service ends. This came amid the 2008 mortgage and foreclosure crisis.
analysis.who_benefits: Servicemembers and their families, particularly homeowners who might face foreclosure or unaffordable mortgage rates when transitioning out of active duty during the housing crisis.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the existing 6% cap on mortgage interest rates from active-duty service only, to one year after service ends, for mortgages and other security interests.
Extends the period of protection against mortgage foreclosure from 90 days after release from service to one year.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and banks would bear the cost of the longer interest rate cap and delayed foreclosure timelines for recently discharged servicemembers.

drawbacks.text: Extending foreclosure protections to one year after service could increase financial risk for lenders, who might respond by tightening credit standards or raising costs for all borrowers.

As drafted, the bill addressed mortgages but left untouched other obligations and debts facing the same servicemembers, meaning the relief was narrow relative to the broader 2008 financial strain on returning troops.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered targeted, modest relief to a specific group of homeowners at real risk of foreclosure during the 2008 housing crisis, at a cost mainly to lenders. However, its protections were narrow—limited to mortgages and to only one year after service—and it never advanced far enough to be evaluated or amended in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee, briefly discharged, then referred to Veterans' Affairs, where it stayed without further action until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Introduced by Sen. John Kerry in March 2008, the bill was referred to the Armed Services Committee and then, in April 2008, discharged and sent to the Veterans' Affairs Committee.
No further legislative action occurred; the bill died in committee when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and banks avoided the extended interest caps and longer foreclosure timelines the bill would have imposed. Servicemembers facing the 2008 foreclosure crisis lost the added protections.

for.name: John F. Kerry
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to extend mortgage interest caps and foreclosure protections for servicemembers.

for.name: 1 Senate Democrat cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill died in committee without any recorded votes or floor debate, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have capped interest rates and delayed foreclosure for recently discharged servicemembers, limiting lenders' collections during the 2008 housing crisis.
